Pool Service Across the Phoenix Area

One free number covers Phoenix and 25 towns and neighborhoods across the Valley. Find your page to read about the water, the homes and the pool rules where you live.

Call (623) 240-0428 How the line works
  1. Home
  2. Service Areas

Pool service in Arizona's biggest metro is local work. The water in Scottsdale is not the same as the water in Surprise, a Sun City backyard is not a Queen Creek lot, and each city writes its own rules about where pool water may drain.

The line answers calls from anywhere in the Phoenix metro, mostly in Maricopa County plus San Tan Valley, Apache Junction and the city of Maricopa in Pinal County. It has no offices: it transfers your call to an independent pool company that takes calls for your area. The pages below explain what is different about each place, with sources.

North Valley and Scottsdale area

North Phoenix, the foothill towns and Scottsdale, from older central neighborhoods to desert lots under the mountains.

Pool service in North Phoenix

The northern City of Phoenix villages, from North Mountain to North Gateway, on hard city water and City of Phoenix pool rules.

Read the North Phoenix page

Pool service in Scottsdale

Scottsdale Water delivers mostly CAP and SRP surface water, with hardness from 16 grains per gallon north to 25 in the south.

Read the Scottsdale page

Pool service in Paradise Valley

Town incorporated in 1961 around one acre lots, served by several water companies, with many homes on septic below Camelback and Mummy Mountain.

Read the Paradise Valley page

Pool service in Fountain Hills

Planned town founded in 1970 on hillsides below the McDowell Mountains, with very hard EPCOR water and strict rules keeping pool water on the lot.

Read the Fountain Hills page

Pool service in Cave Creek

A desert foothills town that runs its own water utility on Central Arizona Project water piped from the canal.

Read the Cave Creek page

Pool service in Carefree

A small desert town whose own water company, overseen by the Town Council, delivers mostly CAP water.

Read the Carefree page

Pool service in Anthem

An unincorporated master-planned community on Interstate 17 whose EPCOR water reports about 18 grains per gallon of hardness.

Read the Anthem page

East Valley and Pinal County edge

Tempe, Mesa, Chandler and Gilbert, the fast-growing southeast and the Pinal County communities beyond them.

Pool service in Tempe

Tempe draws about 87 percent of its water from the Salt and Verde rivers, and requires five foot pool fences by city code.

Read the Tempe page

Pool service in Mesa

Mesa sorts tap water hardness by zone, about 12 to 16 grains on average, and wants pools drained to the sewer cleanout.

Read the Mesa page

Pool service in Chandler

Chandler blends Salt, Verde and Colorado River water with groundwater, averaging 16.5 grains of hardness, and grew from 30,000 people in 1980.

Read the Chandler page

Pool service in Gilbert

Incorporated in 1920 and still a town, with water that blends SRP and CAP supplies averaging 8 to 10 grains of hardness.

Read the Gilbert page

Pool service in Ahwatukee

A City of Phoenix urban village south of South Mountain, first built in the 1970s and annexed by 1987.

Read the Ahwatukee page

Pool service in Queen Creek

A fast-growing former farm town in Maricopa and Pinal counties, incorporated in 1989, on well water of 6 to 17 grains.

Read the Queen Creek page

Pool service in San Tan Valley

A Pinal County community of over 100,000 that voted in 2025 to become a town on July 1, 2026.

Read the San Tan Valley page

Pool service in Apache Junction

Straddles Maricopa and Pinal counties below the Superstition Mountains, with two hard water providers, SRP power and many winter residents.

Read the Apache Junction page

Pool service in Maricopa

A young Pinal County city, incorporated in 2003, that grew from about 1,000 residents to roughly 73,300.

Read the Maricopa page

West Valley

Glendale, Peoria and the newer cities spreading west along Interstate 10 and north along the Loop 303.

Pool service in Glendale

West Valley city whose tap water blends Salt and Verde river water, Colorado River water through CAP, and city wells.

Read the Glendale page

Pool service in Peoria

Long West Valley city that shares Colorado River water and the Pyramid Peak treatment plant with Glendale for its northern neighborhoods.

Read the Peoria page

Pool service in Surprise

Surprise runs its own water utility while EPCOR serves some addresses, and city rules keep drained pool water off streets.

Read the Surprise page

Pool service in Sun City

Community served by EPCOR water, where this page covers private backyard pools rather than the recreation center pools.

Read the Sun City page

Pool service in Litchfield Park

Founded in 1916 as a Goodyear cotton town, with hard Liberty Utilities well water and streets of palms and orange trees.

Read the Litchfield Park page

Pool service in Goodyear

Grew from 65,275 to 95,294 residents in the decade to 2020, with Interstate 10 splitting water service between the city and Liberty Utilities.

Read the Goodyear page

Pool service in Avondale

Avondale blends Colorado River water delivered through Phoenix with city well water, so mineral levels at the tap can shift.

Read the Avondale page

Pool service in Buckeye

Buckeye's city water comes only from wells in the Hassayampa sub-basin, and three different providers serve parts of the city.

Read the Buckeye page

Pool service in Laveen

Former farm and dairy country between South Mountain and the Salt River, partly a Phoenix village and partly unincorporated county.

Read the Laveen page

What changes from one town to the next

  • The water you fill with. Cities blend river water from the Salt and Verde, Colorado River water from the Central Arizona Project and groundwater in different amounts, so hardness differs.
  • Where pool water may go. Cities set their own rules for draining and backwashing; many send it to the sewer cleanout or your own yard and never to the street.
  • Pool barrier rules. Fence and gate requirements are set locally.
  • Utilities. Electricity comes from APS or SRP depending on the address, which matters when a storm knocks out power to the pump.
  1. Call the numberAn automated assistant answers (623) 240-0428 day or night, weekends included.
  2. Describe the poolSay what is going on: cloudy or green water, a pump that hums, a heater that will not fire, scale on the tile, and which part of the Valley you are in.
  3. Get put throughThe call is transferred to an independent, locally owned pool service company, which hears a short summary of the problem before it picks up.
  4. Deal with them directlyThat company looks at the pool, quotes, does the work and bills you. If it cannot answer, your name, number, area and problem are passed along so it can call you back.

Common questions

Does the line have an office in my town?

No. Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro has no offices or crews anywhere. It is a phone line that transfers your call to an independent, locally owned pool company that takes calls for your area.

My town is not listed. Can I still call?

Yes, if you are in the Phoenix metro. The towns with their own page are the ones where people search for pool service most. Call, say where you are, and the assistant will try to connect you with a company that works there.

Why do pool rules change from town to town?

Each city and town sets its own rules for things like where drained or backwashed pool water may go and how pools must be fenced, and water providers differ, so the hardness of the water you fill with differs too. Each town page covers what applies there.

Wherever you are in the Valley, call the free line

One free call at any hour. Say what the pool is doing and where in the Valley you live, and the line puts you through to an independent, locally owned pool company that sees the pool for itself and sets its own price.

Call (623) 240-0428
